chapter: New Orleans bands, Oliver and Armstrong
title: Perhanis's scheme of social and economic change in jazz styles
summary: In one long statement Perhanis traces jazz from the recording industry's star system through swing, bebop and Miles Davis turning his back on the audience. Rose answers that he will comment in general.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: It would be fair to say that due to economic, social, political circumstances, that jazz went through various changes in forms from, let's say, what I'm familiarly, what I primarily call traditional jazz or New Orleans jazz, went through changes to, let's say, in the mid-30s swing, and then up through bebop or bop style, and then the so-called progressive jazz, all these different styles, due to various changes in the social structure. For instance, let me just give you one example. Would it be fair to say that when the black American moved north, they had to fit into an economic structure, not only because they had to survive, but because it produced its rewards, financial rewards. They had to fit into an economic structure which, due to the recording industry, which was becoming certainly more prevalent at this time, it just started and then it became much larger. And the recording industry was interested in getting stars. It had a star system, and so you got the individual to be predominant instead of the group, because if you could star a Louis Armstrong, then it was, you know, you could bill him as the greatest trumpet player, whatever it is. That this pressure to conform to the standards of the recording industry changed, literally changed, the whole style of the music. So that, let's say, Louis Armstrong playing Stardust, with either the Carol Dickinson or Louis Russell orchestra in the background, playing a kind of just a sweet, insipid sort of ensemble riff style, with Louis doing all his magnificent solo playing. But when you put the whole thing together, you have a kind of a strange hybrid of sweet dance music, a kind of a Guy Lombardo sweet dance music, juxtaposed to a jazz soloist, in a form which would never occur if it wasn't for the fact that Louis had to play the sweet stuff, but never at the same time gave up his true jazz origins. And then the only way in which sweet band music, or what I would call popular dance music, and jazz ever came together in any kind of a successful form, would be in the so-called swing period of the 30s, in which you get this, what I would call successful combination of jazz and sweet dance music. And then by the 40s, things have changed politically and economically, well, certainly politically and socially so much, that, for instance, a black man was becoming aware of himself in a way in which there was quite a bit of conscious rebellion and protest against the society at large. And you get this phenomenon of Miles Davis playing with his back to the orchestra, in which now the division between player and audience had become so great, which I don't think existed at all. In the early New Orleans time, there was hardly any division between audience and player. And literally, they were one. It was very much a folk art, I would say. But by the 40s, you have this tremendous division, not only because the jazz player is now playing in a stage setting, but there's a purpose, literally turning your back to the audience, which is kind of symbolizing Miles Davis. And the music begins, music in a way reflects that kind of a political protest in the way, let's say, Charlie Parker plays, or the so-called cool sound, which certainly isn't a happy extroverted music. Now, I just went through three stylistic changes with the political stuff. Now, do you...
Let me comment in general. Okay. Just comment in general on that kind of a scheme.
